findings.matters: Material financial improvement in the council's position during a period of budget pressures and immediately before merger into a unitary authority, showing proactive debt management

findings.detail: Housing is the council's most significant operational and financial challenge. The government subsidy for temporary accommodation remains capped at 90% of 2011 Local Housing Allowance rates, creating a persistent shortfall between actual costs and recoverable subsidy that the council quantifies at £1.4 million per year. Homelessness demand remains consistently high, though PPTA placements have fallen to 484 households (down 27 from last year).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this service can become self-sustaining or whether it will continue draining reserves. The structural subsidy gap is a permanent feature of the business case, not a cyclical pressure.

findings.quote: there remains a significant funding gap between the cost of providing temporary accommodation and the subsidy recoverable from central government. It is estimated that, if subsidy levels reflected current LHA rates, the Council would receive approximately £1.4 million of additional income annually

findings.headline: Inconsistent policies and procedures continue to contribute to control weaknesses despite some progress
findings.detail: A recurring theme across multiple audits is the lack of clear, consistently-applied documented policies and procedures. While some progress has been made in follow-up audits, weaknesses in this area continue to contribute to several partial and minimal assurance opinions, affecting business continuity.
findings.matters: Without documented, consistently-applied policies, controls cannot function reliably. This systemic weakness means the council's processes cannot be relied upon to operate consistently.
findings.figures: Recurring theme contributing to multiple partial and minimal assurance opinions
findings.quote: A recurring theme identified through our audit work remains the inconsistent availability and application of documented policies and procedures. While some progress has been demonstrated, particularly in follow-up audits, weaknesses in this area continue to contribute to several partial and minimal assurance opinions.

findings.paper_title: HBC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26 Annex A
findings.headline: Only 50% of high-priority audit actions were implemented in the year; a decline from the previous year
findings.detail: Internal Audit tracks implementation of high-priority agreed actions. In 2025/26, only 50% were confirmed as implemented by due date, against a target of 95%. This is described as a decrease from the previous year and reflects ongoing challenges services face in implementing improvements amid organisational pressures.
findings.matters: Non-implementation of audit recommendations means identified control weaknesses are not being fixed. This pattern suggests either weak management commitment or genuine inability to execute improvements — both material concerns for lenders.
findings.figures: 50% implementation rate of high-priority actions; target 95%
findings.quote: During 2025/26, 50% of high-priority actions were confirmed as implemented within the year. Although progress has been made, this represents a decrease from the previous year and underscores the ongoing challenges services face in implementing agreed improvements amid broader organisational pressures.

findings.paper_title: HBC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26 Annex A
findings.headline: Limited organisational capacity and competing demands may affect the council's ability to sustain improvements and respond to audit findings
findings.detail: The report identifies that limited capacity and competing priorities may affect the council's ability to sustain improvements, respond promptly to audit findings, and support ongoing audit activities. This is specifically noted as a risk to the control environment. Organisational Resilience (Impact of Savings Plans) also received partial assurance.
findings.matters: Capacity constraints indicate the council may struggle to implement financial restructuring or improvements — critical for lenders assessing whether the council can execute a turnaround if needed.
findings.figures: Organisational Resilience audit: partial assurance
findings.quote: There is still a risk that limited organisational capacity and competing demands may affect the Authority's ability to sustain improvements, respond promptly to audit findings, and support ongoing audit activities.

findings.paper_title: HBC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26 Annex A
findings.headline: Multiple key financial systems received weak audit opinions: Creditors minimal, Debtors and Cash & Bank partial
findings.detail: Creditors received minimal assurance. Debtors Follow-up, Cash and Bank, and aspects of organisational resilience affecting financial management all received partial assurance, indicating weaknesses that could impact the achievement of financial objectives if not addressed. The report notes further management action is required to strengthen controls.
findings.matters: Weak controls over payables, receivables, and cash create risk of financial statement error and misuse of public funds. Lenders need confidence in the council's financial control environment.
findings.figures: Creditors: minimal assurance; Debtors Follow-up: partial assurance; Cash and Bank: partial assurance
findings.quote: Debtors Follow-up, Cash and Bank, and aspects of Organisational Resilience affecting financial management received partial assurance opinions. Additionally, audits of Creditors (Accounts Payable) and Officer Declarations of Interest, Gifts and Hospitality resulted in minimal assurance opinions, highlighting significant weaknesses in those areas.

findings.paper_title: HBC Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025-26 Annex A
findings.headline: Only partial assurance on governance and internal control; full assurance is not achievable
findings.detail: The Chief Internal Auditor has provided partial assurance, not full assurance, on the council's framework. Section 3.2 notes that while results show improvements compared to 2024/25, partial assurance remains the overall opinion. The variation in audit outcomes shows some progress but also persistent weaknesses.
findings.matters: Partial assurance signals ongoing risks in how the council manages its governance, financial controls, and risk — a key concern for lenders and the finance director assessing council stability.
findings.figures: Partial assurance opinion; mix of substantial (1), reasonable (8), partial (7), and minimal (3) audit opinions across the council
findings.quote: the Chief Internal Auditor can provide partial assurance that the Council has in place an adequate and effective framework of governance, risk management and internal control for the period 1st April 2025 to 31st March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2b. Appendix B - Annual Audit Report - AAR Tracker
findings.headline: Strategic Risk Register does not include financial stability and temporary accommodation crisis, now reported quarterly to Cabinet
findings.detail: Auditor found that the council's Strategic Risk Register does not include key corporate risks including financial stability and the temporary accommodation crisis. This gap in risk identification suggests the council's risk management framework is not capturing its most material exposure. The council now reports strategic risks (including temporary accommodation pressures) quarterly to Cabinet and Overview & Scrutiny.
findings.matters: A council facing a homelessness emergency that is not formally tracked in its risk register suggests governance weakness and potential for unmanaged service escalation. Temporary accommodation is typically a high-cost, volatile area.
findings.figures: None disclosed in tracker
findings.quote: The completeness of the Strategic Risk Register, overseen by the Senior Leadership Team, needs to be reviewed as it does not appear to include key issues for the Council such as financial stability and tackling the temporary accommodation crisis.

findings.paper_title: 2b. Appendix B - Annual Audit Report - AAR Tracker
findings.headline: 2024/25 Group Financial Statements not yet published; auditor flags statutory deadline of 15 January 2026 ahead of 27 February backstop
findings.detail: Hastings has not yet published its 2024/25 Group Financial Statements by the statutory deadline and faces a government backstop of 27 February 2026. The auditor has explicitly flagged that failure will trigger statutory audit powers. The council is strengthening finance capacity (Joint Deputy CFO, business partners) and working with LEC to improve delivery on the 2025/26 accounts, due 30 June 2026.
findings.matters: Missing statutory accounts deadlines signals governance and finance capacity problems. Auditor threat of statutory intervention is a serious escalation indicating loss of confidence in the council's financial reporting controls.
findings.figures: Deadline: 15 January 2026 for 2024/25; backstop 27 February 2026; target 30 June 2026 for 2025/26
findings.quote: Council should produce its 2024/25 Group Financial Statements by 15 January 2026 so that it meets the statutory deadline for publishing the 2024/25 accounts for audit, ahead of the government's backstop date of 27 February 2026. If this is not achieved, then we will consider the use of our statutory audit powers.

findings.paper_title: 2b. Appendix B - Annual Audit Report - AAR Tracker
findings.headline: General Fund Reserve forecast to deplete by 2027 with £7.54m funding gap by 2029
findings.detail: The auditor identifies that current reserve-burning rate is unsustainable. If the council does not reduce reliance on reserves in the 2026/27 budget (due 11 February 2026), the auditor will invoke statutory audit powers. The council acknowledges the problem and is working on recurring savings and transformational change through a dedicated transformation team.
findings.matters: A council depleting its reserves and facing a structural £7.54m funding gap within three years presents material credit risk. This is not cyclical pressure but a sustainability crisis.
findings.figures: General Fund Reserve depletion forecast by 2027; £7.54m funding gap by 2029
findings.quote: if maintained at the current level will deplete the General Fund Reserve by 2027 and leave a forecast funding gap of £7.54m by 2029

findings.headline: Sports Centres shifted from budgeted income to operating loss; reserves drawn to plug £19k gap
findings.detail: Sports Centres were expected to generate £50.7k of income but instead cost £27.4k net—a £78k adverse variance. Reserves of £59k were transferred to partially cover this, but a £19k deficit remained at year-end.
findings.matters: A swing of this magnitude from planned income to operating loss suggests demand collapse or pricing/operational failure. Using reserves to cover ongoing operational deficits is not sustainable and raises questions about recovery or future viability.
findings.figures: Budget (income) £50,710; actual (cost) £27,358; variance £78,068; reserves applied £59,000; final deficit £19,068

findings.headline: Housing Management staff spending underspent by £420k (91% below budget) while housing sector experienced largest overspend
findings.detail: Housing Management & Admin was budgeted at £457k but spent only £36.8k, a £420k (91%) underspend. This scale of underspend suggests significant vacancy, restructuring, or service disruption rather than efficiency, at precisely the time when housing is experiencing its largest overspend.
findings.matters: Severe staffing gaps in housing management during a period of explosive homelessness demand (£1.79m overspend) indicates the council lacks operational capacity to manage its most stressed service.
findings.figures: Budget £457,040; actual £36,811; underspend £420,229

findings.headline: Homelessness service overran budget by £1.79m (32% overspend) with no reserves drawn to cover it
findings.detail: Homelessness cost £7.34m against a budget of £5.55m. Additionally, unbudgeted Homelessness Prevention spending of £210.7k was incurred. No reserves were allocated to manage this overspend, which remains unfunded at year-end.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a structural, ongoing pressure on council finances. An overspend of this magnitude at year-end suggests either inadequate budgeting, uncontrolled demand escalation, or insufficient capacity to manage this service, all of which signal financial risk to lenders.
findings.figures: Homelessness: budget £5,550,459, actual £7,337,429, variance £1,786,970. Homelessness Prevention: actual £210,755 (budget £0).

findings.headline: Commercial property, housing and energy investments carry additional risks requiring adequate reserves to protect service delivery
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that its commercial property, housing and energy investments add risk and volatility to its financial position. It notes the need to maintain sufficient reserves given the totality of risks (unexpected expenditure, income volatility, loans and guarantees, economic downturns, pandemics).
findings.matters: Asset-based investments can suffer impairment, particularly concerning when a council is already running a deficit and relying on investment returns for budget stability
findings.figures: No specific breakdown, but commercial holdings included in the £15-35 million investment range
findings.quote: The additional risks that the Council has taken on with commercial property, housing and energy investments needs to be considered in the context of the totality of risk that the Council faces e.g. unexpected expenditure demands, robustness of income streams, loans and guarantees to other parties, economic downturns, pandemics etc. Where there is more risk and volatility in income streams, the Council will need to ensure that it maintains sufficient reserves to ensure the Council's ability to deliver key services is not jeopardised.

findings.headline: The council is using investment income and commercial property returns to help close its budget deficit
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Strategy explicitly states that investment income can help close the budget gap and preserve services. However, the report warns that over-reliance on such income streams would create unnecessary risks to the council's ability to deliver statutory services.
findings.matters: Income-dependent budget strategies are vulnerable to market volatility and asset impairment; this warning suggests the council recognises a structural mismatch between revenue and expenditure
findings.figures: Council holds £14 million in investments; generally maintains £15-35 million at any one time; investment income was £1.232 million in 2025/26
findings.quote: Investments can help to close the gap in the budget in the years ahead and thus help to preserve services, assist in the regeneration of the town, provide additional housing, and enhance the long-term sustainability of the town. However, over reliance on such income streams would involve taking unnecessary risks with the future of the Council and its ability to deliver statutory services.

findings.headline: Hastings has a financial deficit being addressed through capital programme reductions and asset sales
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes significant reductions to the Capital Programme specifically to help address the council's financial deficit. Asset sales have been agreed as part of this response, with financial stability being the primary focus.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether a council has structural budget problems and how it is managing them; cutting capital spending and selling assets are material responses indicating financial stress
findings.figures: Significant reductions to Capital Programme (quantum not specified in covering report); £65.4m long-term borrowings estimated by end March 2026
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Budget included significant reductions in the Capital Programme to help the Council address its financial deficit including agreeing to asset sales, with the primary focus being on financial stability and addressing the housing crisis.

findings.headline: Loans to Hastings Housing Company total £5.489m, representing contingent council exposure
findings.detail: The council has extended £5.489m in capital loans to its wholly-owned housing company for property purchases. This creates direct council exposure to housing company asset performance and adds to the council's overall liabilities should the company face difficulties.
findings.matters: Loans to council-controlled entities represent contingent liabilities if the housing company's asset values decline or rents underperform
findings.figures: Capital loans to Hastings Housing Company: £5,489,398 as at 31 December 2025
findings.quote: The above table shows a series of loans to the Hastings Housing Company in respect of property purchases. As at 31 December 2025 the Capital loans amount to £5,489,398.

findings.headline: Property fund investment shows £0.5m loss on £5m invested in 2017-2021
findings.detail: The council invested £2m in a CCLA property fund (April 2017) and £3m in a diversified investment fund (2020/21), totalling £5m. By end of 2024/25 these investments were valued at only £4.5m—a 10% loss. This reflects both property market stress and fund management outcomes.
findings.matters: Asset losses on prior investments raise questions about asset management capability and quality of income-generating assets being acquired
findings.figures: 2017 investment £2m; 2020/21 investment £3m; 2024/25 value £4.5m; loss £0.5m (10%)
findings.quote: The Council invested £2m in a property fund (CCLA) in April 2017 and a further £3m tranche of monies in a diversified investment fund in 2020/21. At the end of 2024/25 the value of those Investments was £4.5m.

findings.headline: Solar panel revenue lacks long-term contracts; debt service risk remains unhedged
findings.detail: The council allocates £2.8m for energy generation (solar) but explicitly acknowledges that 'the ability to meet the debt repayments from energy savings and sale of the surplus energy will remain a risk unless long term forward sale agreements are made.' No such agreements are mentioned.
findings.matters: Unhedged revenue streams supporting debt create material refinancing risk if energy prices fall or generation underperforms relative to projections
findings.figures: Energy Generation budget 2026/27: £2.8m (£0.3m expected spend); additional £1.04m allocated for Solar Panels
findings.quote: Some projects such as the solar panel installations have some asset backed values, but the ability to meet the debt repayments from energy savings and sale of the surplus energy will remain a risk unless long term forward sale agreements are made.

findings.headline: Economic downturn would force 'greater service cuts' due to council's income dependency
findings.detail: The CFO warns explicitly that while current borrowing levels are 'not considered excessive', 'a downturn in the economy with resultant loss of income would require the Council to make greater service cuts to balance the budget.' This reveals the vulnerability of a model relying on capital project income in a weak economy.
findings.matters: A recession scenario would force rapid spending cuts when revenue-dependent debt service remains fixed—amplifying financial stress
findings.figures: No specific downturn scenario quantified; based on £15.053m new borrowing dependent on project income
findings.quote: The Council's existing borrowing levels are not considered excessive. However, a downturn in the economy with resultant loss of income would require the Council to make greater service cuts to balance the budget.

findings.headline: Council increasingly dependent on income streams from capital projects to service debt
findings.detail: The CFO explicitly flags that borrowing for economic development and regeneration schemes means the council is now 'increasingly dependent upon the income streams to finance the debt repayments'. This creates vulnerability if housing rents, energy sales, or other project income underperform.
findings.matters: Revenue-dependent debt servicing creates direct operational risk: asset/service underperformance flows directly to debt sustainability
findings.figures: £10m housing acquisitions; £2.8m energy generation; £5.489m existing loans to Housing Company
findings.quote: Where borrowing money to finance economic development or regeneration schemes the Council is increasingly dependent upon the income streams to finance the debt repayments.

findings.headline: Council financing costs consume 10% of Net Revenue Stream with acknowledged risk of rising as funding reduces
findings.detail: Financing costs currently represent 10% of the Net Revenue Stream. The CFO explicitly warns that if the Net Revenue Stream continues to reduce (as forecast in the MTFS), 'the ratio will potentially continue to climb leaving less available for front-line services and placing further pressures on budget positions', even though interest rates are fixed.
findings.matters: A rising ratio of fixed debt service to shrinking revenue leaves less flexibility for services and creates risk in demand shocks or revenue underperformance
findings.figures: Financing costs 2025/26: 10% of Net Revenue Stream
findings.quote: In Hastings's case the ratio of financing costs in 2025/26 represents, 10%, of the Net Revenue Stream which leaves 90% of the revenue stream for all the other services to be provided. The higher the percentage, therefore, the less is left for running services.

findings.headline: New borrowing requirement jumps to £15.053m in 2026/27, more than double 2025/26 actual of £6.681m
findings.detail: The capital programme for 2026/27 requires £15.053m in new borrowing, compared to £6.681m in 2025/26 and £5.055m projected for 2027/28. This represents a significant and sudden jump in annual debt issuance, concentrated in housing acquisitions (£10m of the £12m programme).
findings.matters: Doubling annual borrowing in a single year signals rapid debt accumulation and commits the council to substantially higher future debt service costs regardless of revenue performance
findings.quote: The Council's Capital programme amounts to some £32.5m (£15.1m net of grants and contributions) in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council's long-term investment portfolio showing capital losses, with 10.5% loss on Diversified Income Fund
findings.detail: The council has invested £5m of reserves in longer-period investments: £2m in CCLA Property Fund (down 1.7% from 2017 investment) and £3m in CCLA Diversified Income Fund (down 10.5% from 2019 investment level as at December 2025). The council explicitly states there are 'no proposals to invest more monies for potentially longer periods given the further potential calls on reserves', confirming that reserve drawdown needs are overriding the need for higher-yielding longer-term investments.
findings.matters: These holdings represent ~£5m of earmarked reserves that are underwater and constrained by future borrowing needs. The council cannot add new longer-term investments because it anticipates needing to draw on reserves for capital projects and debt servicing. This reveals a constraint on financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Property Fund capital value down 1.7% (£2m invested April 2017, valued at December 2025); Diversified Income Fund valued at £2,685,903 on 31 December 2025 (10.5% below £3m initial investment); dividend yield on Property Fund 3.2% p.a., Diversified Income Fund 3.02%
findings.quote: There are no proposals to invest more monies for potentially longer periods given the further potential calls on reserves. The monies in these funds can still be obtained relatively quickly should the need arise.

findings.headline: Borrowing limits not increased despite capital programme growth, council relying on historic headroom rather than new approval
findings.detail: The Authorised Limit and Operational Boundary for borrowing were increased by £25m in 2023/24, but remain at that level for 2026/27 onwards despite growing capital expenditure plans. The council justifies this by stating that 'anticipated capital expenditure did not occur when expected' and there is 'sufficient capacity within them already as a result of previous capital expenditure plans that did not commence as planned'. This represents a reliance on historical slippage rather than formal increase in borrowing approval.
findings.matters: Slippage-based headroom is not the same as planned borrowing capacity. If capital projects accelerate or if the planned £15m+ borrowing materialises faster than forecast, the council could quickly approach or exceed the authorised limit, requiring emergency governance action.
findings.figures: Authorised Limit and Operational Boundary both increased by £25m for 2023/24 and held at that level; capital expenditure forecast for 2026/27 £30,903k expected (revised budget £44,386k including slippage carry-forward)
findings.quote: The Authorised Limit and Operational Boundary were both increased by £25m for the 2023/24 financial year. The anticipated capital expenditure did not occur when expected and therefore it is considered that the current levels remain appropriate

findings.headline: MRP charges increasing annually, requiring council to make Voluntary Revenue Provision payments to smooth budget impact
findings.detail: The council changed its MRP policy in 2022/23 which brought short-term revenue savings, but the policy is now producing increasing annual charges. To manage this pressure, the council is making additional Voluntary Revenue Provision (VRP) payments of £80,000 per year for five years (with 2025/26 being year four). This £400,000 will be set aside to reduce the impact of rising MRP in later years, signalling anticipated revenue budget strain.
findings.matters: Rising MRP charges bite into revenue budgets just as the council is scaling up capital expenditure. The decision to pre-fund future years' MRP pressures suggests the council expects revenue budgets to be tight. This is a forward indicator of affordability constraints.
findings.figures: MRP 2025/26 estimated at £1,019,210 (£939,210 MRP plus £80,000 VRP); cumulative VRP overpayments to 31 March 2025 are £240,000 with further £80,000 scheduled for 2025/26
findings.quote: MRP payments will now increase annually placing additional pressure on the revenue budget annually. To alleviate the pressure in the medium term the council has decided to make additional VRP payments of £80,000 per year for 5 years

findings.headline: Constrained reserve depletion forcing substantial new external borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The council has been using internal borrowing (drawing down cash reserves) to avoid external debt, but explicitly states this strategy is now constrained. Capital expenditure plans require new borrowing of £15.1m in 2026/27 continuing into future years, with the Capital Financing Requirement expected to grow from £75.9m to £103.9m by 2028/29. The council identifies that reserves are 'increasingly' being used and this capacity is 'limited'.
findings.matters: This signals a turning point: the council cannot rely on reserves to self-finance capital expenditure any longer. Lenders need to understand the timing and scale of new debt issuance, and whether reserve depletion has left the council with adequate liquidity buffers.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement rising to £103.9m by 2028/29 (from £75.9m in 2025/26); as at 31 December 2025 council balances were £22.2m; new borrowing required £15,053k (2026/27), £5,055k (2027/28), £9,633k (2028/29)
findings.quote: Given that the Council is increasingly using its reserves these need to be readily available and not subjected to unnecessary risk or exposure.

findings.paper_title: 2b202526 Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report DraftV3
findings.headline: Hastings Housing Company (council-owned) is in arrears on interest payments to the council due to cash flow pressures
findings.detail: The council has loaned £5,489,398 to Hastings Housing Company, which is wholly council-owned. The company is required to pay £262,862 annually in interest. The report states: 'due to cash flow pressures, the Housing Company is currently in arrears with its interest payments to the Council. Late payments will be subject to additional interest charges in accordance with the loan agreement.' This indicates financial distress in a material council-controlled entity.
findings.matters: A lender is exposed not just to council solvency but to the financial viability of its major controlled entities. Arrears on loan servicing indicate the Housing Company may be unable to service debt and poses a contingent liability to the council.
findings.figures: Outstanding loans to Hastings Housing Company £5,489,398; annual interest due £262,862
findings.quote: due to cash flow pressures, the Housing Company is currently in arrears with its interest payments to the Council. Late payments will be subject to additional interest charges in accordance with the loan agreement.

findings.paper_title: 2b202526 Annual Treasury Management Outturn Report DraftV3
findings.headline: Council has depleted reserves to avoid external borrowing; future capital expenditure will force borrowing at elevated rates of 5%+
findings.detail: No external borrowing was undertaken in 2025/26; instead, the council financed capital expenditure using cash reserves. The report explicitly states 'the scale of capital expenditure and future programme commitments indicate that borrowing will be required in the short to medium term'. At 31 March 2026, PWLB Certainty Rates were 5.04% for one-year borrowing and 5.72% for ten years. The council's strategy of avoiding borrowing while rates remain elevated has worked in the short term but is explicitly kept under regular review.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know when a council will exhaust its cash reserves and be forced to borrow at prevailing (high) rates, which will materially increase the council's financing costs and debt service burden.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £6.606m; PWLB 10-year rate 5.72%; outstanding PWLB debt £63,397,500; investments held £18.432m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: the scale of capital expenditure and future programme commitments indicate that borrowing will be required in the short to medium term. In the interim, the use of internal resources namely reserves and balances has provided a cost-effective means of financing capital expenditure

findings.headline: All medium-term financial planning limited to 2027-28 due to Local Government Reorganisation decision expected Spring 2026; no forecasts beyond due to 'material changes'
findings.detail: Council deliberately produces MTFS only to 2027-28, stating that LGR discussions are expected to reach decision point in Spring 2026 and will likely involve 'material changes' that cannot be forecast. This eliminates strategic financial planning beyond two years, preventing visibility of council's sustainability across a normal multi-year capital and revenue planning horizon.
findings.matters: Lenders typically require multi-year financial visibility to assess sustainability; LGR could substantially alter council's funding, service scope, and financial position; inability to forecast beyond 2028 limits confidence in any commitments extending beyond that date
findings.figures: MTFS forecasts only to 2027-28; LGR decision expected Spring 2026
findings.quote: The MTFS in Appendix B has intentionally only been produced up until 2027/28 as this is the expected date of the changes involving LGR discussions. No further predictions have been made after this date due to the fact that there is likely to be material changes and this will need to be worked through once a final decision is known.

findings.headline: Full business rates reset in April 2026 will revalue all properties to 2024 rental prices with new tiered multipliers, creating income forecast volatility
findings.detail: Valuation Office Agency revaluation exercise on 1 April 2026 will update all rateable values and introduce new tiered multipliers, including lower rates for retail, hospitality and leisure. Council's income forecasting depends on assumptions about appeals and collection rates; this major structural change creates one-off uncertainty in income that underpins the balanced budget assumption. Transitional relief will attempt to minimize sharp increases but effects on specific sectors and property sizes unpredictable.
findings.matters: Business rates are material component of funding base; major revaluation creates unpredictability in income forecasts that support the balanced budget; appeals can create large backdated liabilities
findings.figures: Full revaluation to 2024 rental values; new tiered multipliers including lower retail/hospitality/leisure rates; transitional relief scheme to follow
findings.quote: The baseline for retained business rates will be reset in full in 2026-27. The reset involves a major revaluation exercise on the 1st April 2026, which will update rateable values (RV's) to reflect 2024 rental prices, alongside new tiered multipliers.

findings.headline: Council committing to additional £331k annual Discretionary Housing Payments funding, entirely self-funded from council resources
findings.detail: Council proposes increasing DHP funding by £331,486 annually to support vulnerable residents facing housing costs, a 2.5-fold increase from current allocation. The council explicitly acknowledges 'Hastings Borough Council will be solely responsible for funding the additional amount'. This new commitment is added during a period when the council is achieving budget balance only through aggressive £517k savings, and represents policy-driven additional spending that must compete with other priorities.
findings.matters: Additional recurring £331k unfunded spending commitment during period of fiscal constraint; unusual countercyclical policy choice; future funding for successor Crisis Resilience Fund (from April 2026) not yet confirmed
findings.figures: £331,486 additional annual DHP funding; 2.5x increase from current allocation
findings.quote: If this recommendation is approved, Hastings Borough Council will be solely responsible for funding the additional amount of £331,486.

findings.headline: £517k savings are built into 2026-27 surplus forecast, but council's historical achievement rate is 80%, with 2025-26 expected to be lower
findings.detail: The council projects a £440k surplus for 2026-27, entirely dependent on achieving £517k in PIER (Priority Income & Expenditure Review) savings. However, the council explicitly notes its 'historical savings achievement rate is around 80%' and 'in 2025/26 that outcome is expected to be lower'. A 20% shortfall would mean £103k of planned savings unachieved, eliminating most of the projected surplus.
findings.matters: Forecast surplus is thin and relies wholly on savings delivery; declining savings performance track record increases risk that the budget tips into deficit
findings.figures: £517k savings required for balance; £440k forecast surplus; 80% historical achievement rate; expected to decline further in 2025-26
findings.quote: The council's historical savings achievement rate is around 80%. However, in 2025/26 that outcome is expected to be lower.

findings.headline: Housing costs (42% of budget) created £692k adverse variance in 2025-26; demand remains consistently high despite prevention and acquisitions programmes
findings.detail: Homelessness is the council's single largest service cost at 42% of net expenditure. The council forecast 470 households in Privately Procured Temporary Accommodation (PPTA) for 2025-26 but started the year with 535 households, creating a £692k adverse variance. Despite running a £12m housing acquisitions programme and prevention work, the council states demand 'continues to be consistently high' and acknowledges that the 'greatest financial risk to the organisation' remains housing, with 'considerable progress' still required to address unmet need built up before 2023.
findings.matters: Single service dominates council budget; forecast error of 14% (65 households) generated £692k variance; repeat of similar variances would eliminate the entire £440k projected surplus
findings.figures: Housing = 42% of £16.9m net expenditure budget; started 2025-26 with 535 PPTA households vs forecast 470; period 3 adverse variance £692k; average PPTA cost £393.57/week
findings.quote: Housing continues to pose the greatest financial risk to the organisation, with changes having a material impact on the outturn. The reason for this is because it currently accounts for 42% of the total net expenditure budget for the Council.

findings.headline: General reserves £3.09m above minimum requirement, but policy permits drawing this down
findings.detail: General Reserve stands at £7.09m against £4m minimum as at 31 March 2025. However, policy states 'The Council will not hold significant balances above those required by the Medium-Term Financial Strategy', leaving discretion to reduce this buffer.
findings.matters: Shows healthy headroom now but policy language permits reserves to be drawn to minimum level if budget pressures emerge; matters to lenders assessing financial resilience
findings.figures: £7.09m actual vs £4m minimum; £1.75m (10% net expenditure), £1m unforeseen events in minimum calculation
findings.quote: The Council will not hold significant balances above those required by the Medium-Term Financial Strategy.

findings.headline: Council has created specific reserve for migration control costs
findings.detail: Item 19 of earmarked reserves lists 'Controlling Migration – Funding for Migration Control', indicating the council has identified and is funding migration-related costs as a discrete budget item.
findings.matters: Shows a council-specific local pressure with cost implications that may not affect other councils; relevant to understanding council's specific demand drivers
findings.figures: Reserve created but amount not stated in policy
findings.quote: 19 – Controlling Migration – Funding for Migration Control.

findings.headline: Council maintains redundancy reserve for expected future staff reduction costs

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 P7 Financial Update Report to end of October 2025
findings.headline: Housing temporary accommodation overspend of £965,299 is structural and will persist
findings.detail: The council started 2025/26 with 535 households in privately procured temporary accommodation against a budgeted 470, a gap of 65 households that was not forecast. Although initial progress was made, placements rose again in September (+19) and October (+21). The problem is not the cost per placement (stable at £392–£393 per week) but volume. Social housing move-ons have collapsed to just 3 lettings in October, down from 19 in January, due to delays at the Hyde Group development and waiting for new homes to complete.
findings.matters: This is a structural overspend, not cyclical. The council's starting assumption about demand was wrong by 65 households, and supply-side constraints (capital project delays, social housing completions) are beyond its control within this financial year. A lender needs to know that housing reserves usage will continue until more homes complete.

findings.paper_title: Hastings BC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - Final (add as supplementary)
findings.headline: No-overall-control administration since 2022; Green Party minority administration formed after 2024 election, creating political uncertainty in budget decisions.
findings.detail: Hastings has been under no overall control since 2022. Following the May 2024 election, a Green Party minority administration formed to run the council. The auditor flags this in the context of difficult budget decisions that will be needed in 2026/27. Minority administrations typically lack the votes to pass budgets unilaterally and require cross-party support or opposition abstention. The council's budget crisis is about to collide with electoral uncertainty (shadow unitary elections May 2027), creating potential gridlock on budget-setting.
findings.matters: A minority administration cannot unilaterally implement the difficult savings and service reductions the auditor identifies as necessary. If opposition groups will not support harsh cuts, the council may drift toward the February 2026 deadline without a balanced budget, triggering auditor statutory powers.

findings.paper_title: Hastings BC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - Final (add as supplementary)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation proposal submitted in September 2025 creates medium-term uncertainty in financial planning and service delivery.
findings.detail: In September 2025, Hastings submitted a joint Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) proposal to central government alongside all East Sussex district and borough councils and the county council. Shadow unitary council elections are scheduled for May 2027. The council has been modelling transitional costs and identifying invest-to-save opportunities as part of LGR planning. This structural change creates uncertainty in medium-term financial planning and creates a two-year window during which normal business continuity must be maintained while governance and finance teams manage reorganisation. The Chief Executive has been shared with Lewes and Eastbourne councils since November 2024.
findings.matters: LGR creates a shadow period of uncertainty (2027 to 2028/29 vesting date) during which the council must continue to deliver services and manage finances, but leadership and resources may be diverted to reorganisation. If the council's financial position deteriorates during this period, the incoming unitary authority inherits a stressed legacy. Lenders need to understand this adds volatility.
findings.figures: LGR proposal submitted September 2025; shadow council elections May 2027; three-year Medium-Term Financial Plan extends to 2028/29 (overlapping with vesting)
findings.quote: In September 2025, in response to Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), the Council submitted its joint LGR proposal to central government, alongside all local district and borough councils and East Sussex County Council (ESCC). Elections for a shadow unitary council will be held in May 2027.

findings.paper_title: Hastings BC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - Final (add as supplementary)
findings.headline: Internal Audit gave only 'Partial Assurance' opinion for 2024/25, with 7 of 10 audits receiving partial assurance ratings due to recurring control weaknesses.
findings.detail: The Council's Internal Audit function gave an overall annual opinion of 'Partial Assurance' for 2024/25 rather than the stronger 'Adequate Assurance'. Seven out of ten audits received 'Partial Assurance' ratings, indicating recurring control weaknesses across the Council. Coverage included key financial systems, corporate governance, and high-risk operational areas such as Temporary Accommodation and Contract Management. Contract Management and Temporary Accommodation were both flagged as partial assurance.
findings.matters: Partial assurance is a below-standard rating signalling that controls are not operating as intended. Multiple partial assurance ratings across key financial systems and operational areas suggest systemic control weakness, not isolated incidents. A council with recurring control failures cannot be relied upon to manage material financial risks effectively.

findings.paper_title: Hastings BC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - Final (add as supplementary)
findings.headline: Strategic Risk Register is not being reported to Cabinet or Audit Committee, and temporary accommodation and financial stability are missing from the register.
findings.detail: The Council's Strategic Risk Register is reviewed monthly by Senior Leadership Team but there is no evidence it was reported to Cabinet or Audit Committee in 2023/24 or 2024/25, despite the Annual Governance Statement claiming it was. The register does not include two of the Council's key priorities: temporary accommodation and financial stability, both of which are material risks. The auditor has raised a Key Recommendation (KR3) requiring quarterly reporting to Cabinet and annual assurance reporting to the Audit Committee, with urgent steps to remedy the absence of reporting in prior years.
findings.matters: If the council's most senior members (Cabinet) are not seeing the Strategic Risk Register, they cannot make informed decisions or allocate resources to mitigate material risks. The absence of temporary accommodation and financial sustainability risks from the register is a clear control failure given these are the council's two most pressing operational challenges.

findings.quote: The SRR shows 12 strategic risks but there is no mention of two of the Council's key priorities, temporary accommodation and financial stability. Our Key 2023/24 recommendation on the significant weakness on the lack of quarterly reporting of the Strategic Risk Register to Cabinet and the annual assurance to Audit Committee continues, as neither of these occurred during 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Hastings BC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - Final (add as supplementary)
findings.headline: 2024/25 financial statements published three months late with a pattern of non-compliance and finance capacity constraints affecting audit delivery.
findings.detail: Hastings shared its draft 2024/25 accounts with auditors on 9 October 2025, three months after the statutory deadline of 30 June. This is part of a pattern: 2023/24 September, 2022/23 August, 2021/22 September. The Council's finance team has struggled with recruitment and vacant posts throughout the year, creating insufficient capacity at critical times. The auditor has raised a Key Recommendation (KR4) requiring publication of the full group accounts by 15 January 2026, warning that failure to meet this date will trigger consideration of statutory audit powers. The finance team's one-person dependency on responding to audit queries has caused delays in providing information.
findings.matters: Statutory accounts publication is a hard deadline in local authority law. Repeated slippage signals either weak finance function capacity or loss of control. A council that cannot produce timely accounts for its own auditor cannot be relied upon for timely financial reporting to creditors or lenders.

findings.headline: Hastings Housing Company Ltd decision deferred to December 2025; £5.5m loan and £0.77m accrued interest
findings.detail: The council holds a £5.5m loan to its subsidiary Hastings Housing Company Ltd and has accumulated £0.77m in accrued interest over three years. An independent external review has been completed but the decision on whether to dissolve the company or bring it back in-house was deferred for Cabinet consideration in December 2025. The uncertainty materially impacts financial reporting: if the company is not a going concern, the accounting treatment and credit-loss provisions on the loan change; if dissolved, group accounts are not required. The 2024/25 financial statements cannot be finalised until this decision is made.
findings.matters: A £5.5m subsidiary loan on a council with depleting reserves is material. If the subsidiary is insolvent or wound up, the council may have to write down the loan. The decision deferral has already delayed accounts publication and creates accounting uncertainty that auditors cannot resolve until the decision is taken.

findings.paper_title: Hastings BC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - Final (add as supplementary)
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs have spiralled to £7.8m with further demand growth forecast but savings programmes underperforming.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation overspent by £7.8m in 2024/25, a 19.3% variance and the main driver of the £210k overall General Fund overspend. The council budgeted for 470 privately procured temporary accommodation (PPTA) households in April 2025 but started the year at 535. Forecast growth is expected to require an additional £1.7m in 2025/26. The Priority, Income & Efficiency Review (PIER) programme achieved only 55% of its £1.266m savings target in 2024/25 (down from 80% in 2023/24), and for 2025/26 the target was reduced to £417k. Despite preventative work preventing 209 homelessness cases and £1.2m in costs since April 2024, planned savings are insufficient to offset escalating costs.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off spike but an embedded demand pressure growing faster than the savings programme can deliver. A 65-household variance from forecast (535 vs 470) was not captured in financial planning, exposing weak forecasting. With homelessness trending upward nationally, this pressure will only intensify and consume an increasing share of net budget.

findings.quote: Rising homelessness expenditure remains a critical concern, prompting the creation of a Homelessness taskforce and engagement with Government for additional funding. Homelessness demand is forecast to grow further, in 2025/26, requiring an extra £1.7m budget allocation.

findings.paper_title: Hastings BC Auditors Annual Report 2024-25 - Final (add as supplementary)
findings.headline: The General Fund Reserve will be exhausted by 2027/28 with a £7.5m budget gap by 2029.
findings.detail: Hastings has drawn down approximately £3m of reserves annually since 2018/19 to cover recurring budget shortfalls. The General Reserve is projected to fall from £5.4m in 2024/25 to £1.7m by 2026/27, with full depletion expected by 2027/28. Without significant savings, additional income, or service reductions, the Council faces unsustainable spending levels. The auditor has raised a Key Recommendation stating that if reserves reliance is not reduced for the 2026/27 Budget Council meeting on 11 February 2026, they will consider using statutory audit powers.
findings.matters: A council relying on reserves to fund recurring spending is unsustainable and signals it cannot deliver a balanced budget from resources. Full reserve depletion means no buffer for any unplanned pressure, making the council unable to meet statutory duties or respond to demand shocks.

findings.quote: the current MTFS contained in this report does not include any future savings that will be proposed as part of the consultation and only currently includes previous savings targets agreed as part of the previous budget setting process

findings.headline: General Reserve projected to fall below the council's £4m statutory minimum in 2027-28
findings.detail: The council's general reserve balance is forecast to deplete from £6.9m (2025-26) to £3.0m by end of 2027-28, breaching its own minimum threshold. This leaves the council with a £957k shortfall against its safety floor and eliminates financial buffer for any adverse movements.
findings.matters: A lender will view breach of minimum reserves as a material governance failure and loss of financial resilience; it removes headroom for any demand shocks or income loss.
findings.figures: General Reserve Balance: 2025-26 £6,947k → 2026-27 £5,674k → 2027-28 £3,043k. Minimum required: £4,000k.
findings.quote: it is estimated that the Council will drop below its minimum General Reserve balance of £4m in the 2027/28 Financial year

findings.paper_title: Updated 2025-26 P3 Financial Update Report to end of June 2025
findings.headline: General Reserve forecast to be drawn down by £430,261 more than originally budgeted
findings.detail: The budget anticipated minimal use of the General Reserve (£29,000). The forecast now shows use of £459,261, a deterioration of £430,261. The projected closing balance of £6.4m remains above the £4m minimum policy, but the significant adverse movement indicates emerging financial pressure.
findings.matters: While reserve coverage is still adequate, a £430k deterioration in forecast reserve use shows the council is under tighter budget control than anticipated and has less contingency capacity than expected.
findings.figures: £29,000 originally budgeted vs £459,261 forecast use (£430,261 adverse variance); £6.4m projected closing balance; £4m minimum recommended
findings.quote: Outturn for the 12 months to 31st March 2026 is an adverse variance to budget of £430,261, following use of budgeted and unbudgeted reserves.

findings.paper_title: Updated 2025-26 P3 Financial Update Report to end of June 2025
findings.headline: Council drawing £304,760 from unbudgeted earmarked reserves to cover current-year overspends
findings.detail: Direct service expenditure is running £735k over budget; the council is using unbudgeted earmarked reserves to partially offset this shortfall, including £237,000 from the Renewal & Repairs reserve and £55,000 from the Green Investment Fund. This supplements the budgeted reserve use.
findings.matters: Tapping unbudgeted reserves to cover revenue overspends erodes financial flexibility and signals budget variance management; using capital and investment reserves for revenue pressures is a warning indicator for lenders.
findings.figures: £304,760 unbudgeted reserve use; £735,023 total direct service overspend; £237,000 from Renewal & Repairs; £55,000 from Green Investment Fund
findings.quote: The unbudgeted use of the earmarked reserves in the 12 months to 31st March 2026 totals £304,760.

findings.paper_title: Updated 2025-26 P3 Financial Update Report to end of June 2025
findings.headline: Housing showing £691,763 overspend (11.6%) driven by higher temporary accommodation placements than budgeted
findings.detail: At budget-setting the council forecast 470 households in privately procured temporary accommodation (PPTA) for April 2025, but started the year with 535. Despite achieving record monthly reductions (15 households in June), the elevated starting position means the service will overspend for the full year. Weekly costs per placement remain stable at £392–£393.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a mandatory service with highly variable demand; a £691k forecast overspend on what should have been a lower baseline indicates budget planning challenges and leaves little margin when demand fluctuates.
findings.figures: 535 households actual vs 470 forecast at year start; £691,763 overspend; 15-household reduction in June (record monthly reduction); £392.34–£393.57 average weekly cost per placement
findings.quote: The main reason for this is a higher number of households living in privately procured temporary accommodation (PPTA) at the start of the financial year than we had forecast in the budget, when it was set in December.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 P3 Financial Update Report to end of June 2025
findings.headline: Direct service expenditure is 4.4% above budget (£735,023 adverse), with Housing the primary driver but Environment & Operations also showing significant variance.
findings.detail: Beyond the £691,763 housing overspend, Environment & Operations shows a £156,132 adverse variance that the narrative does not explain in detail, and Commercial Services a £47,410 overspend. The council has partially mitigated these through earmarked reserves but the fact that a range of service areas are running above budget suggests broad-based cost pressures or forecast error rather than isolated issues in one service.
findings.matters: Multi-service overspends suggest either structural cost growth, weakened cost control, or strategic budget under-estimation. This pattern is more concerning than isolated service variance.
findings.figures: Direct Service Expenditure £735,023 adverse (4.4%); Environment & Operations £156,132 adverse; Commercial Services £47,410 adverse
findings.quote: The forecasted outturn for the 12 months to 31st March 2026 is an adverse variance to budget of £735,023 for direct service expenditure. However, this is partially offset by a use of unbudgeted earmarked reserves.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 P3 Financial Update Report to end of June 2025
findings.headline: One-off property credits of £199,038 from 2019 balancing charges are helping offset the underlying structural overspend.
findings.detail: The Property and Commercial Assets service reports a £186,465 underspend after reserves, driven almost entirely by a £199,038 favorable variance from historical service charge credits and VAT corrections on properties dating back to 2019. This is non-recurring income. Without this, the service position would be adverse and the council's total outturn position would be materially worse.
findings.matters: Councils relying on one-off items to balance budgets face deteriorating positions in the following year. This suggests the underlying operational position is weaker than the headline variance suggests.
findings.figures: £199,038 favorable from property credits; £186,465 net underspend after reserves in Property and Commercial Assets
findings.quote: The Properties and Estates service is showing a favourable variance of £199,038, this is largely due to credits received for service charges on a number of properties dating back to 2019 which comprise end of year balancing charges and corrections for VAT incorrectly charged.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 P3 Financial Update Report to end of June 2025
findings.headline: General Reserve draw £0.46m against £0.029m budgeted—a £0.43m overshoot driven by service cost pressures.
findings.detail: The council budgeted to draw only £29,000 from general reserves but forecast an actual draw of £459,261—15 times higher. This is the net position after using £304,760 of unbudgeted earmarked reserves (from Renewal & Repairs and Green Investment Fund) to partially offset the £735,023 service overspend. Notably, £237,000 of the earmarked drawdown covers unfinished works from 2024/25, suggesting carry-forward cost pressures. The general reserve will close at £6.4m, still above the £4m minimum policy floor, but the cash movement is material and shows budget-setting risk.
findings.matters: Reserve drawdown above budget indicates either cost forecast error or real cost escalation requiring cash management. For lenders, this is a leading indicator of whether a council's medium-term financial plan will hold.
findings.figures: Forecast General Reserve draw £459,261 vs budgeted £29,000 (£430,261 adverse variance); unbudgeted earmarked reserves used £304,760; closing General Reserve £6.4m vs £4m minimum; opening balance £6.853m
findings.quote: The current 2025/26 use of the General Reserve is expected to be £0.46m. This is £0.43m above the budget agreed by Council in February 2025.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 P3 Financial Update Report to end of June 2025
findings.headline: Housing temporary accommodation overspend of £691,763 driven by higher-than-budgeted demand.
findings.detail: The council started the financial year with 535 households in privately procured temporary accommodation (PPTA), 35 more than the 470 forecast when setting the budget. This structural mismatch means even with reductions of 10 households per month (their target), the overspend will persist through the year. Weekly placement cost remained stable at £392.34–£393.57, so the issue is volume not price. The council is making progress—15 households were housed in June (their highest monthly reduction ever) and they now sit below the prior-year position—but the starting imbalance created an unavoidable £691,763 overspend.
findings.matters: Welfare costs are structural service obligations and housing pressure is a live policy challenge for lenders to council budgets. This shows the council's budget-setting underestimated demand by 7% in April and is now reliant on housing acquisitions and prevention work to manage the trajectory.
findings.figures: £691,763 overspend; 535 households in PPTA vs 470 forecast; £392.34–£393.57 weekly placement cost; 15-household reduction in June; national PPTA rose 19% in 24/25, Hastings only 8%
findings.quote: The main reason for this is a higher number of households living in privately procured temporary accommodation (PPTA) at the start of the financial year than we had forecast in the budget, when it was set in December. At the point the budget was set we had 500 households in PPTA and set a forecast for the remainder of 24/25 of a reduction of 10 households a month. We therefore forecast having 470 households in PPTA at the start of April. However, due to higher-than-expected need for temporary accommodation we started the financial year at 535 households.

news_drafts.headline: Hastings forecasts £596k net overspend for 2026/27, to be met from the General Reserve
news_drafts.lead:
Hastings Borough Council forecasts a net overspend of £596,000 for 2026/27, to be funded from the General Reserve after earmarked reserves and other budget adjustments. The September (period 6) monitoring report to Cabinet shows £759k of overspend before earmarked reserves are applied. The paper says a draw on the General Reserve was not expected when the balanced budget was approved.

Housing reports a £390,000 overspend for the year. The 2026/27 budget assumed 350 households would need privately procured temporary accommodation by March 2027; the paper puts the number at 462, with 590 households in temporary accommodation of all kinds at the end of September. It attributes the overspend to demand above the budget assumption, says placement numbers are showing signs of stabilisation, and says a review of the Housing budget and its cost drivers has started.

Cemetery and Crematorium is forecasting a £96.7k overspend from lower-than-expected cremation numbers and reduced income, which the paper links to a national decline in deaths and the growth of direct cremation providers. Salary slippage in the Street Cleansing direct services organisation partly offsets it, leaving Environment and Operations £78.4k over. The Chief Legal Officer and Monitoring Officer's area forecasts a £252.9k overspend, attributed to higher legal costs, increased caseloads and agency staff covering vacancies, alongside temporary transition costs of a new shared service with Lewes District Council.

news_drafts.headline: Hastings Council reschedules £11m debt for £2.3m lifetime savings
news_drafts.lead: Hastings Council has identified £2.3 million in lifetime savings by refinancing six loans worth £11 million, the Full Council heard on Wednesday. The council will take advantage of early repayment discounts worth £5 million to reduce replacement funding to less than £6 million, generating annual savings of around £515,000 in the first two years. The Treasury Management Update reported an additional £2.9 million net present value benefit from the restructuring. The move is part of efforts to strengthen financial resilience ahead of Local Government Reorganisation in April 2028. The council's longer-term pooled fund investments, meanwhile, have declined by approximately £562,000 from their initial cost, though the funds continue to generate dividend income of nearly 5 per cent and 3 per cent respectively.
